To find the last digit in base 6, we need the remainder when 355 is divided by 6.

\(355 \div 6 = 59\) remainder \(1\), since \(6 \cdot 59 = 354\).

So the base-6 representation of 355 ends in **1**.

#### 1

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 2010s, and it remains just as impressive years after its release. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, the movie turns the origin story of facebook into something far more interesting than a simple tech biography. instead of treating the rise of a social media empire as a triumphal success story, it presents it as a tense, bitter, and deeply human drama about ambition, betrayal, loneliness, and the cost of genius.

one of the film’s greatest strengths is its screenplay. sorkin’s dialogue is fast, precise, and often hilarious, but it also carries real emotional weight. the conversations feel like verbal duels, with characters constantly trying to outthink, outmaneuver, or wound one another. even when the film is packed with technical or legal details, it never feels dry. every scene has momentum, and every exchange reveals something important about power and insecurity. the script is especially effective because it refuses to simplify its characters into heroes and villains. mark zuckerberg is brilliant, arrogant, defensive, and often cruel, but he is also lonely and socially alienated in a way that makes him strangely sympathetic. eduardo saverin, sean parker, and the winklevoss twins are all given enough dimension to feel real rather than symbolic.

jesse eisenberg gives a remarkable performance as mark zuckerberg. he captures the character’s intelligence and impatience with extraordinary precision, but what makes the performance memorable is the emotional undercurrent beneath the rapid speech and cold exterior. eisenberg plays mark as someone who is always trying to stay ahead of everyone else, yet never fully belongs anywhere. there is a sadness in the performance that keeps the character from becoming merely obnoxious. andrew garfield is equally strong as eduardo saverin, bringing warmth, loyalty, and eventual heartbreak to the role. his performance gives the film its emotional center, especially as the friendship between eduardo and mark deteriorates. armie hammer is excellent in the dual role of the winklevoss twins, and his scenes add both humor and a sense of old-money entitlement. justin timberlake, as sean parker, brings charisma and danger to the film, making him feel like a seductive force of disruption.

fincher’s direction is meticulous and controlled, which suits the story perfectly. he creates a world that feels sleek, cold, and emotionally detached, yet never lifeless. the visual style reinforces the themes of isolation and ambition. the film’s opening scene, a rapid-fire conversation between mark and erica in a harvard bar, immediately establishes the pace and tone: intelligent, cutting, and emotionally bruising. throughout the movie, fincher uses framing, lighting, and editing to emphasize the characters’ distance from one another, even when they are in the same room. the result is a film that feels intimate and clinical at the same time.

the score by trent reznor and atticus ross is another major achievement. it is eerie, propulsive, and modern, giving the film a restless energy that matches the story’s emotional tension. the music does not simply support the scenes; it shapes the atmosphere, making the rise of facebook feel less like a celebration and more like the beginning of something unsettling. the soundtrack is one of the reasons the film feels so contemporary and so psychologically sharp.

what makes the social network especially effective is that it understands that the story is not really about technology. it is about human relationships under pressure. facebook becomes a symbol of connection, but the film is full of people who are unable to connect honestly with one another. mark wants recognition and control, eduardo wants loyalty, sean wants influence, and the winklevoss twins want credit and status. everyone is chasing something, and in the process they damage the relationships that matter most. that emotional contradiction gives the film its power.

the pacing is excellent, and the structure, which moves between the founding of facebook and the legal fallout, keeps the story dynamic. the courtroom framing device adds tension without making the film feel like a conventional legal drama. instead, it creates a sense of inevitability, as if the audience is watching a tragedy unfold from the beginning. that tragic quality is one of the film’s most interesting aspects. by the end, mark has achieved enormous success, but he is also more isolated than ever. the final image of him refreshing erica’s friend request is simple, devastating, and unforgettable.

if there is any criticism to make, it is that the film’s style and intelligence can sometimes create emotional distance. some viewers may find the characters too cold or the dialogue too relentless. the movie is not interested in warmth or easy catharsis, and that can make it feel emotionally austere. but that austerity is also part of its brilliance. the film knows exactly what it is doing, and it commits fully to its vision.

overall, the social network is a masterfully made film: smart, tense, beautifully acted, and deeply observant about ambition and alienation in the digital age. it is both a portrait of a specific moment in tech history and a timeless story about friendship, power, and the price of success. it is one of those rare films that feels intellectually stimulating and emotionally resonant at the same time, and it deserves its reputation as a modern classic.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 2010s, and it remains impressive because it is not really about facebook so much as it is about ambition, loneliness, status, betrayal, and the cost of being brilliant but emotionally disconnected. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, the film turns a relatively recent business story into something that feels almost shakespearean in its bitterness and scale.

one of the movie’s greatest strengths is its screenplay. sorkin’s dialogue is fast, precise, and often cutting, but it never feels empty or showy for its own sake. every conversation seems to carry multiple layers at once: legal maneuvering, personal resentment, intellectual one-upmanship, and insecurity. the film’s structure, which moves between depositions and flashbacks, gives the story a sense of inevitability. we already know that relationships have broken down and lawsuits have begun, so the tension comes from watching how those fractures formed.

jesse eisenberg gives a remarkable performance as mark zuckerberg. he plays him not as a simple villain or genius, but as someone deeply intelligent, socially awkward, defensive, and hungry for recognition. eisenberg captures the character’s speed of thought and emotional distance in a way that makes him fascinating even when he is difficult to like. his mark is not a cartoon of tech arrogance; he is more unsettling than that because he feels plausible. he seems like someone who can build something world-changing while failing to understand the human damage he causes along the way.

andrew garfield is equally strong as eduardo saverin, bringing warmth, hurt, and dignity to a role that could have been reduced to the betrayed friend. his emotional arc gives the film much of its heart. the friendship between mark and eduardo is one of the movie’s most tragic elements, because it begins with genuine loyalty and shared excitement, then slowly collapses under pride, mistrust, and power. garfield makes eduardo’s sense of betrayal feel deeply personal.

armie hammer’s dual performance as the winklevoss twins is another standout. the casting and visual effects work together so well that the twins become more than a technical gimmick. they represent privilege, entitlement, and a certain polished confidence that contrasts sharply with mark’s abrasive intelligence. their scenes add both humor and tension, and they help broaden the film’s social landscape.

fincher’s direction is controlled and elegant. he gives the film a cold, precise atmosphere that matches the emotional distance of the characters and the sterile world of elite universities, boardrooms, and legal offices. the cinematography, editing, and production design all contribute to a mood of sleek unease. even when the film is visually restrained, it never feels dull. instead, it feels meticulously calibrated. every shot seems designed to reinforce the idea that these people are always calculating, always positioning themselves.

trent reznor and atticus ross’s score is essential to the film’s identity. the music is haunting, modern, and slightly ominous, giving the story a pulse that feels both technological and tragic. it helps transform scenes of coding, meetings, and arguments into something almost mythic. the score does not overwhelm the film; it deepens it.

what makes the social network especially effective is that it understands how modern power often emerges from a mix of talent, timing, ruthlessness, and insecurity. the film does not present success as clean or heroic. instead, it shows how innovation can be inseparable from exploitation and how the desire to be “the one who got there first” can destroy relationships. it is a movie about creation, but also about ownership, resentment, and the emotional emptiness that can accompany victory.

if there is a criticism to make, it is that the film is so tightly focused on its central figures that some broader social and ethical questions remain in the background. the movie is less interested in facebook’s long-term cultural consequences than in the personal drama behind its origin. for some viewers, that may feel like a limitation. but for me, it is also part of the film’s strength: by narrowing its focus, it becomes more intimate and more devastating.

overall, the social network is a brilliant film: intelligent, stylish, emotionally sharp, and endlessly rewatchable. it captures a specific moment in the rise of digital culture while also telling a timeless story about friendship, envy, and the need to matter. it is one of those rare movies that feels both of its time and larger than it.

the social network is one of those rare films that feels both sharply entertaining and quietly devastating. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, it turns the creation of facebook into something much bigger than a tech origin story. at its core, the movie is about ambition, resentment, loneliness, status, and the way intelligence can become a weapon when it is mixed with insecurity.

what makes the film so effective is that it never treats mark zuckerberg as a simple villain or genius. jesse eisenberg plays him as brilliant, awkward, defensive, and emotionally sealed off. he is not especially likable, but he is fascinating because the film understands that his coldness is part of the tragedy. he wants recognition, but he cannot connect with people in a normal way, so he builds a platform that connects everyone else. that contradiction gives the movie its emotional power.

the screenplay is one of the best things about it. sorkin’s dialogue moves at a relentless pace, full of wit, precision, and tension. even scenes of people talking in rooms feel like high-stakes confrontations. the film jumps between depositions and flashbacks, which gives the story a fractured, almost forensic structure. this is not just a rise-and-fall narrative; it is a story being reconstructed through competing versions of events. that choice makes the movie feel smarter and more morally complicated than a standard biopic.

fincher’s direction is equally important. he gives the film a cold, controlled visual style that matches the emotional distance of the characters and the digital world they are creating. the cinematography is sleek and restrained, often using dark interiors, muted colors, and precise framing to create a sense of isolation. even when the characters are surrounded by people, they often seem alone. that visual loneliness is one of the film’s strongest qualities.

the performances are excellent across the board. eisenberg is perfectly cast, but andrew garfield is the film’s emotional heart as eduardo saverin. his performance brings warmth, hurt, and betrayal into the story, and his scenes give the movie its most human stakes. armie hammer, playing both winklevoss twins with the help of digital effects, is surprisingly effective as the embodiment of privilege and entitlement. justin timberlake also stands out as sean parker, bringing charisma and danger to a character who understands how to turn youthful idealism into power.

one of the film’s greatest achievements is that it makes the founding of facebook feel like a modern american myth, but a bitter one. instead of celebrating innovation in a triumphant way, it shows how success can be built on exclusion, manipulation, and emotional damage. the movie is not really about coding or entrepreneurship; it is about the social cost of winning. every major relationship in the film is damaged by ego, and every victory seems to leave someone more isolated.

the score by trent reznor and atticus ross deserves special praise. it is eerie, propulsive, and emotionally unsettling, adding a sense of unease that runs beneath the entire film. the music helps transform what could have been a straightforward drama into something more haunting and modern. it feels like the sound of a new era being born, but not necessarily a better one.

if the film has a weakness, it is that its style and intelligence can sometimes create emotional distance. some viewers may find it hard to fully sympathize with any of the characters, and the movie is more interested in sharp observation than in deep warmth. but that distance is also part of its design. the film is about people who are always calculating, always performing, and always protecting themselves.

overall, the social network is a brilliant, tightly constructed, and deeply memorable film. it captures a specific moment in the rise of social media, but it also speaks to timeless human flaws: envy, ambition, betrayal, and the need to be seen. it is stylish without being empty, smart without being smug, and emotionally colder than many great dramas, yet somehow more haunting because of it. it remains one of the defining films of its era.

Mia took a deep breath and pushed down on the pedals. The bike moved forward a little. Then it tipped. Dad caught her before she fell.

Mia laughed. “That was funny!”

They tried again and again. Each time, Mia stayed on a little longer. She learned to balance better. She learned to start slowly. She learned to keep going even when she felt shaky.

After a while, Dad held the bike less and less.

“Ready?” he asked.

Mia nodded.

She pushed the pedals, looked straight ahead, and moved forward. Dad let go.

Mia noticed something wonderful: she was moving on her own!

“I did it!” Mia shouted.

Dad clapped. “Yes, you did!”

the social network is one of those rare films that feels both sharply entertaining and quietly devastating. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, it turns the creation of facebook into something much bigger than a tech origin story. at its core, it is a movie about ambition, loneliness, status, betrayal, and the way genius can be tangled up with insecurity and cruelty.

what makes the film so effective is how it refuses to treat mark zuckerberg as a simple hero or villain. jesse eisenberg plays him as brilliant, defensive, socially awkward, and deeply wounded by rejection. his mark is not warm or especially likable, but he is fascinating because the film understands that his intelligence and his emotional immaturity are inseparable. he wants to be admired, but he also seems to resent the very people whose approval he craves. eisenberg’s performance is precise and fast, full of nervous energy and cutting wit, and it gives the movie its sharp edge.

the screenplay is one of the film’s greatest strengths. sorkin’s dialogue moves like a machine gun, but it never feels empty. every conversation is loaded with power struggles, ego, and subtext. even scenes that are mostly people talking in rooms feel tense and dramatic. the script also does something clever: it makes the audience care about code, business deals, and legal disputes without ever losing sight of the emotional stakes. the lawsuits are not just about money or ownership; they are about who gets credit, who gets left behind, and who gets to tell the story of success.

fincher’s direction is perfectly suited to this material. his style is controlled, cold, and meticulous, which matches the film’s themes of calculation and alienation. the visual design is sleek and often dark, with a palette that makes the world of harvard, offices, and deposition rooms feel both prestigious and emotionally sterile. the camera movement is subtle but purposeful, and the editing gives the film a relentless momentum. even when the story jumps around in time, it never feels confusing. instead, the structure adds to the sense that the past is being reconstructed through competing versions of events.

the supporting cast is excellent across the board. andrew garfield brings real emotional depth to eduardo saverin, making him more than just the betrayed business partner. his hurt feels genuine, which makes the conflict more painful. justin timberlake is surprisingly effective as sean parker, capturing the charm and recklessness of someone who knows how to sell a dream while ignoring the damage he causes. armie hammer’s dual performance as the winklevoss twins is both technically impressive and thematically fitting, since the film is so interested in duplication, identity, and the idea of being replaced.

one of the film’s smartest choices is that it never tries to make facebook seem morally simple. it shows the platform as an invention that is both transformative and troubling. the movie does not need to predict every consequence of social media to understand that the desire for connection can be turned into a system of competition, performance, and surveillance. that gives the film a lasting relevance. even though it is set in the early days of facebook, it feels even more resonant now, when online identity and social validation are more central than ever.

the score by trent reznor and atticus ross deserves special praise. it is eerie, propulsive, and emotionally unsettling in exactly the right way. the music gives the film a sense of forward motion while also suggesting something hollow underneath the surface. it helps turn what could have been a straightforward business drama into something more haunting.

if the film has a weakness, it is that its emotional distance can sometimes feel intentional to the point of chilliness. some viewers may wish for more warmth or a deeper sense of the broader cultural impact of facebook beyond the central characters. but that coldness is also part of the film’s design. it mirrors the emotional isolation of its protagonist and the transactional nature of the world he helps create.

overall, the social network is a superb film: intelligent, stylish, and emotionally sharp. it works as a legal drama, a character study, and a cautionary tale about the cost of turning human connection into a product. it is one of the defining films of its era, and it remains compelling because it understands that the most important battles are often not about technology itself, but about ego, belonging, and the need to matter.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 2010s, and it remains impressive because it is not really about facebook alone. it is about ambition, resentment, status, loneliness, and the way genius can be tangled up with cruelty. david fincher directs it with a cold, precise confidence that makes every scene feel controlled, tense, and alive. the result is a movie that feels both intimate and epic, even though much of it is built from conversations in offices, dorm rooms, and legal depositions.

one of the film’s greatest strengths is its screenplay by aaron sorkin. the dialogue moves with extraordinary speed and intelligence, but it never feels like empty cleverness. every exchange reveals character, power, or insecurity. mark zuckerberg’s words are especially memorable because they are written as both defensive and revealing: he is brilliant, socially awkward, wounded, and often deeply unpleasant, yet the film never reduces him to a simple villain. instead, it presents him as someone who is constantly trying to outrun humiliation. that complexity gives the movie its emotional force.

jesse eisenberg gives a remarkable performance as mark. he captures the character’s restless energy, impatience, and emotional distance without turning him into a caricature. his mark is not a cool tech visionary in the usual hollywood sense; he is prickly, insecure, and often difficult to like, which makes him more interesting. andrew garfield, as eduardo saverin, provides the film’s emotional center. his performance is warmer and more openly vulnerable, and that contrast makes the betrayal at the heart of the story hit harder. armie hammer, playing both winklevoss twins, is also excellent, bringing a polished arrogance that fits the film’s world of privilege and entitlement.

the film’s structure is another major achievement. by framing the story through legal disputes and flashbacks, it turns the rise of facebook into a kind of modern tragedy. the audience already knows that success has come at a cost, so the suspense comes not from whether mark will succeed, but from how badly relationships will fracture along the way. this structure also gives the movie a bitter irony: the creation of a platform meant to connect people is shown as a process that isolates and damages nearly everyone involved.

fincher’s direction is meticulous. he uses dark interiors, reflective surfaces, and a restrained visual style to create a world that feels sleek but emotionally cold. the pacing is brisk, yet the film never feels rushed because every scene has purpose. the editing is especially strong, helping the movie jump between timelines and perspectives without losing clarity. the soundtrack by trent reznor and atticus ross is equally important. it adds a pulsing, uneasy atmosphere that makes the film feel modern and haunted at the same time.

what makes the social network endure is that it understands the emotional cost of success in the digital age. it is not a celebration of innovation, and it is not a simple condemnation either. instead, it shows how a culture obsessed with speed, competition, and visibility can reward people who are willing to sacrifice empathy. the film’s final image of mark refreshing a page, waiting for a response that may never come, is quietly devastating. for all the money, power, and influence he gains, he is still alone.

if there is a criticism to make, it is that the film’s intelligence can sometimes create emotional distance. its characters are fascinating, but not always inviting. some viewers may wish for more warmth or a broader social perspective beyond the elite circles the movie focuses on. still, that narrowness feels intentional, and it suits the story being told. the film is less interested in the whole history of facebook than in the emotional and moral logic behind its creation.

overall, the social network is a brilliant, stylish, and deeply unsettling film. it combines superb writing, outstanding performances, and masterful direction into a story that feels both specific to its moment and timeless in its themes. it is one of those rare movies that is as entertaining as it is insightful, and it leaves you thinking not just about technology, but about the human need for recognition, belonging, and power.
